title: Median of Sorted Sequences Problem

content.problemStatement:
Task: Two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 are already sorted in non-decreasing order. The task is to output the median of the multiset formed by combining both arrays.

For an odd total number of elements, the median is the middle value. For an even total, it is the arithmetic mean of the two middle values. At least one array is non-empty.

Design a solution with O(log(min(m, n))) time complexity (binary search on the smaller array), where m and n are the input lengths.
constraints: nums1 and nums2 are sorted in non-decreasing order
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of arguments: [nums1, nums2]. Example: [[1,3],[2]]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialized floating point number (median).
notes: Preferred solution: binary search on the smaller array to partition both arrays so that left partitions contain the lower half of elements.
Carefully handle empty arrays and even/odd combined lengths.
Watch for integer overflow when computing sums of large integers; compute median using max/min and divide using double precision.
Judge compares numeric results with standard double precision tolerance.

sampleTestCases.explanation: Combining and ordering the values gives [1, 2, 3]. With three values, the middle value 2 is the median.
The combined ordered sequence is [1, 2, 3, 4]. Its two middle values are 2 and 3, so the median is (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

hidden.label: Median lies after several smaller-array elements
Integer overflow precision check with max 32-bit integers
Integer underflow precision check with min 32-bit integers
Valid partition at smaller-array left boundary
Valid partition at smaller-array right boundary
Disjoint range: all elements in nums1 smaller than nums2
Disjoint range: all elements in nums1 larger than nums2
Single element in one array, many in other
Odd total with a high-valued second array
One array contains all larger elements

notes: All hidden test cases are concrete arrays and numeric expected outputs.
The checker compares floating point results with standard double precision tolerance (e.g., 1e-6).
Preferred algorithm: binary search partition on the smaller array to achieve O(log(min(m,n))) time.

solution.approach: Binary-search partition on the smaller array: choose cut i in nums1 (0..m) and cut j = (m + n + 1)/2 - i in nums2 so that left partitions contain the lower half. Ensure maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1. If condition fails, move binary search left or right. Compute median from max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2) and min(minRight1, minRight2). Use double arithmetic for even totals.
notes: Handle empty arrays by treating out-of-range left/right values as +/-infinity when computing maxLeft/minRight.
When computing the average of two large integers, convert to double before dividing to avoid integer overflow.
Edge cases: one array much shorter than the other; duplicates; negative numbers; arrays with identical values.

optimal.description: Use binary search on the smaller array. Let m = len(nums1), n = len(nums2). Ensure nums1 is the smaller. Binary search i in [0..m]. Set j = (m + n + 1)/2 - i. Define maxLeft1 = (i==0)? -inf : nums1[i-1]; minRight1 = (i==m)? +inf : nums1[i]; similarly for nums2 with j. If maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1, partition is correct. If total is odd, median = max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2). Else median = (max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2) + min(minRight1, minRight2)) / 2.0. Use double arithmetic for the final result.

hints: Binary search on the smaller array reduces complexity to O(log(min(m,n))).
Compute j from i so that left partitions contain half the elements.
Use sentinel values for out-of-range partition edges to simplify comparisons.
followUps: How would you find the k-th smallest element (generalization) in O(log(min(m,n))) time?
If arrays are stored on disk and random access is expensive, how would you adapt the approach?
How to extend to more than two sorted arrays (median of k sorted arrays)?
